definition: A phenomenon where a neural network represents more distinct features than it has neurons, by encoding multiple features in overlapping, entangled combinations of neuron activations.
details: Superposition is a key challenge for mechanistic interpretability, since it means individual neurons often don't cleanly correspond to single, human-understandable concepts, complicating efforts to reverse-engineer model behavior.

explainer.lead: A phenomenon where a network represents more distinct features than it has neurons by encoding features in overlapping, entangled combinations of activations. It matters because it is a central obstacle to mechanistic interpretability.

tiers.eli5: Like packing many labelled items into fewer boxes by overlapping them, so you can't point to one box and say it holds just one thing.
tiers.practitioner: Interpretability engineers must use sparse or dictionary-based methods rather than reading single neurons; the pitfall is assuming one neuron equals one concept when activations are entangled.
tiers.paperLevel: Features outnumber neurons and are stored in overlapping combinations of activations; there is no clean one-to-one neuron-to-concept mapping, complicating reverse-engineering of model behavior.

explainer.example: A neuron that fires for both 'cat' and 'round' inputs illustrates two features sharing one activation channel rather than a single clean concept.
